1. Executive Summary

This report analyzes how generative AI (GenAI) tool usage affects student academic outcomes across 50,000 students spanning five major categories (STEM, Business, Humanities, Medical, Arts). The analysis examines three strategic questions: (1) the relationship between GenAI usage hours and GPA change/skill retention, (2) how this relationship varies by academic discipline, and (3) whether institutional policies and prompt engineering skills moderate AI's impact on learning.

Top Three Findings

  • GenAI usage shows a weak negative correlation with GPA change (r = -0.05) and moderate negative with skill retention (r = -0.12), while being strongly correlated with AI dependency (r = 0.67). The relationship follows a quadratic pattern suggesting diminishing returns beyond ~12 hours/week.
  • STEM students are the heaviest AI users (10.5 hrs/week) and show the largest GPA gains (+0.217). Debugging/Troubleshooting drives positive outcomes; Direct Answer Generation correlates with GPA declines (-0.066).
  • Prompt engineering skill is the strongest predictor of positive outcomes. Advanced users outperform Beginners by +0.063 GPA points regardless of policy. "Allowed with Citation" policies outperform "Strict Ban" on every metric.

2. Dataset Overview

The dataset contains 50,000 student records with 16 variables covering demographics, GenAI usage patterns, academic performance, and wellbeing. Data quality is exceptional: zero missing values, zero duplicates, all values within plausible ranges. Minor artifacts include GenAI hours capped at 40.0 (ceiling effect) and study hours floored at 1.0, with negligible impact given the large sample.

3. Analytical Framework

The analysis follows a structured five-stage workflow ensuring rigour, transparency, and reproducibility:

  • Description — Initial dataset exploration, variable identification, and data quality assessment.
  • Inquiry — Formulation of 10 analytical questions, prioritised to 3 strategic questions.
  • Goal Design — Detailed analytical plans with data subsets, metrics, visualisations, and robustness checks.
  • Execution — Full statistical analysis: correlations, regressions, ANOVA, chi-square, 20+ tables and visuals.
  • Synthesis — Cross-cutting integration into actionable strategic recommendations.

This framework ensures each finding is traceable from raw data through analysis to recommendation, with documented assumptions and robustness checks at every stage.

Track 2: Majors, AI Dependency, and Outcomes

Compared GenAI usage patterns and outcomes across five major categories using ANOVA with Tukey HSD post-hoc tests. ANOVA confirms significant differences (F = 32.27, p < 0.001). STEM significantly differs from all other majors (p < 0.001).

Use case patterns are strikingly discipline-specific: 52% of Humanities students use AI for Copywriting/Drafting, 52% of STEM for Debugging/Troubleshooting, 48% of Business for Ideation, and 48% of Medical for Summarizing/Reading.

One-size-fits-all AI policies ignore fundamentally different use patterns across disciplines. Disciplinary AI literacy programs should reflect these differences.

Key results: Both Policy (F = 46.29, p < 0.001) and Skill (F = 561.47, p < 0.001) independently predict GPA outcomes. Strict Ban policies correlate with higher anxiety (4.89 vs 4.12) and higher burnout (29.8% High vs 23.8% under Allowed). Chi-square confirms the policy-burnout association (p < 0.001).

Prompt engineering skill is the strongest predictor of positive AI outcomes — surpassing both usage volume and institutional policy. Bans are associated with higher anxiety and burnout without improving GPA.

5. Cross-Domain Insights and Implications

Emerging Opportunities

  • AI as a learning accelerator in STEM — Debugging-focused GenAI use correlates with higher GPA gains and skill retention, suggesting AI functions as an effective learning tool when used for problem-solving.
  • Skill development as a lever — Prompt engineering skill's strong predictive power indicates teachable competencies can significantly improve AI outcomes, making this a high-ROI intervention target.

Emerging Risks

  • The 'Direct Answer Trap' — Students using AI primarily for direct answer generation show the worst outcomes (-0.066 GPA penalty). This pattern is most common among high-dependency users.
  • Policy backfire potential — Strict Ban policies do not reduce AI usage meaningfully (8.37 vs 8.42 hrs/week) but are associated with higher anxiety, higher burnout, and lower GPA gains.

Unexpected Finding

Despite a strong correlation between GenAI hours and self-reported dependency (r = 0.67), dependency itself has a negligible direct effect on GPA. The mechanism through which AI affects grades is mediated by how students use it (use case and skill level) rather than how much they rely on it.

6. Strategic Recommendations

Recommendation 1: Invest in AI Literacy Training Over Restrictions

Prompt engineering skill is the single strongest predictor of positive outcomes across every major and policy context. Universities should develop mandatory AI literacy programmes focused on effective prompting, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and discipline-specific use cases. Estimated impact: +0.06 GPA points (Beginner to Advanced), ~3x the effect of policy changes.

Recommendation 2: Adopt Discipline-Specific AI Guidelines

Blanket AI policies ignore fundamentally different use patterns. STEM should encourage debugging use; Humanities should develop writing guidelines emphasising editing over generation; Medical programmes should focus on summarisation. This targeted approach could close the ~0.02 GPA gap between top- and bottom-performing disciplines.

Recommendation 3: Replace Bans with Structured Allowed-Use Frameworks

"Allowed with Citation" outperforms "Strict Ban" on every metric: higher GPA gains (+0.208 vs +0.187), lower anxiety (4.12 vs 4.89), lower burnout. Institutions should transition to citation-based frameworks that teach responsible AI use rather than driving it underground.

9. Methodological Note

This analysis employed a structured five-stage workflow (Description, Inquiry, Goal Design, Execution, Synthesis) designed for analytical rigour, transparency, and traceability. Each finding can be traced from raw data through specific analytical steps to the final recommendation.

Statistical methods: Pearson correlations, OLS linear and quadratic regression, one-way/two-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD, Kruskal-Wallis tests, chi-square tests, and descriptive group comparisons. Tools: Python 3.12 with NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, Statsmodels, Matplotlib, and Seaborn.

Dataset: 50,000 records, 16 variables, zero missing values. Sensitivity checks included outlier exclusion, non-parametric alternatives, and bootstrapped confidence intervals. Results are robust at the 95% confidence level.

All source code, generated tables (CSV), and visualisations (PNG) are available as supplementary materials alongside this report for full reproducibility.
